newsitem.title: UK: Major versus Blair, a contrast in campaign styles.
newsitem.headline: Major versus Blair, a contrast in campaign styles.

text.p: When the cabin crew of John Major's campaign jet donned tartan caps and ginger wigs to be photographed with the prime minister on a flight back from Scotland, the first reaction of reporters on board was: Labour leader Tony Blair would never have allowed this.
By their campaigns shall you know them.
Opinion polls suggest the past month spent criss-crossing Britain will not have a bearing on the outcome of Thursday's election. Labour is still projected to win handsomely.
But the fascinating contrast in style between the two main protagonists in what has been a media-driven, quasi-presidential campaign has spoken volumes about the state of their parties.
Major, with nothing to lose, has been, in his own words, liberated. He has plunged into crowds with relish, clearly glad to escape his Conservatives' eternal wrangling over Europe.
"I love it. This is what politics is all about," he beamed last Friday as he was mobbed by cheering Bangladeshis in Whitechapel, one of the poorest parts of London.
Blair, by contrast, has run a disciplined, safety-first campaign designed to protect his big poll lead, where even the spontaneity has seemed scripted.
Major is undoubtedly his party's strongest suit. But critics say he has strayed too often from its second-best card: the government's economic record over the past five years.
Above all, with Britain seemingly in the mood for a change, Major has failed to persuade voters to forgive broken promises not to raise tax and, crucially, the party's splits over Europe.
This issue above all has defined the Conservative campaign, just as it has dominated Major's 6-1/2 years as prime minister.

The most gripping moment of the election was on April 16 when Major, facing a revolt by over 200 Conservative candidates against his wait-and-see stance on the European Union's planned single currency, made a passionate, unscripted appeal to them.
"Like me or loathe me, do not bind my hands when I am negotiating on behalf of the British nation," he said.
It was a moment worthy of a Shakespearean tragedy, with Major finally realising that he had sown the seeds of his own fall from power by failing to stand up to his Euro-sceptics.

So great is Labour's thirst for power that Blair has had no difficulty keeping his own Euro-sceptics quiet, allowing him to stick to a meticulously choreographed campaign that -- though he would deny it -- has been more style than substance.

After a mid-campaign wobble when Major scored a few hits, Blair quickly regained his confidence and injected some much-needed passion into his stump speech setting out how Labour could make a difference after 18 years of Conservative rule.

Although some commentators complain that this is still an impersonal string of abstract nouns -- 'decency', 'vision', 'compassion', 'trust' -- the speech succinctly conveys what Blair himself says is his chief asset: his sense of purpose.

"The difference between Labour and the Conservatives is that we want the whole nation to prosper, not just a few people at the top," he told several hundred Labour supporters who had braved the rain in Rochdale, northwest England, last Saturday.
Conversations with Labour voters over the past month suggest there is more respect than affection for Blair in the party.
"We'll vote for him, but I just wish he was a bit more Old Labour," said Lynn MacDonald of Perth, Scotland. "Labour should be more about narrowing the gap between the rich and the poor."
Pressure like this within Labour ranks could presage problems for Blair if he does win on Thursday. Less than 48 hours before polling, his momentum looks unstoppable.
Major, meanwhile, insists everything is still to play for.
He dismisses polls auguring a Labour landslide and bristles at suggestions that a farewell feel has crept into his campaign.

One of life's battlers, he will not give up until the last vote is counted. Labour's election theme is 'Things can only get better'. Not to be outdone, the song played on the final flight of Major's campaign on Monday was 'Simply The Best' by Tina Turner, who, as Major said, is no stranger to comebacks.
